title: The Magi, King Herod, and the Flight to Egypt
summary: Magi from the east follow a star to Jerusalem, asking where the newborn king of the Jews is, and King Herod, alarmed, learns from the scribes that the Messiah is to be born in Bethlehem. The Magi find the child, worship him, and present gold, frankincense, and myrrh, then return home by another route. Warned in a dream, Joseph flees with Mary and Jesus to Egypt while Herod massacres the boys of Bethlehem; after Herod's death the family settles in Nazareth in Galilee.
story: Chapter 1 established who Jesus is: son of David, son of Abraham, Immanuel. Chapter 2 shows how the world receives him. Gentile foreigners come to worship; the reigning king of the Jews tries to kill him; and Jerusalem's religious experts know exactly where the Messiah should be born but do not go to see. The chapter is built around places, Bethlehem, Egypt, Ramah, and Nazareth, and each is tied to a prophecy, as though Jesus' earliest movements retrace Israel's own history. The child who goes down to Egypt and is called out again will soon pass through the waters of baptism and be tested in the wilderness (chapters 3 and 4), reliving Israel's story as its true Son.
historical:
Herod the Great ruled as king of Judea under Rome from 37 BC until his death, usually dated to 4 BC (a minority of scholars argue for 1 BC). He was an Idumean, from a family that had converted to Judaism, and many Jews never accepted him as a legitimate king. He was a great builder, rebuilding the Jerusalem temple on a grand scale and constructing fortresses and the port of Caesarea, and he was ruthlessly suspicious. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the late first century, records that he executed his wife Mariamne, three of his own sons, and many others he feared as rivals. A report of a newborn king of the Jews would have been intolerable to him.

Josephus does not mention the killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and some historians doubt it for that reason. Others note that Bethlehem was a small village, so the number of children under two may have been perhaps a dozen or two, a crime small enough to escape notice among Herod's larger atrocities, and that the act fits everything Josephus says of his character. After Herod's death his kingdom was divided: Archelaus ruled Judea and Samaria, and was so harsh that Rome deposed him in AD 6, while his brother Herod Antipas ruled Galilee, which explains why Joseph chose to settle there.
cultural:
The Magi (Greek magoi) were originally a priestly class among the Medes and Persians, and by this period the word was used for sages, interpreters of dreams, and astrologers in the East, often associated with Babylon and Persia. Matthew does not say how many there were or that they were kings; the tradition of three kings grew later from the three gifts and from Psalm 72:10-11 and Isaiah 60:3-6, which speak of kings bringing gifts. Gold, frankincense (an aromatic resin burned as incense), and myrrh (a fragrant resin used in perfume, medicine, and burial) were costly gifts fit for royalty, and many of them came from Arabia. Later Christians saw in them tributes to Jesus as king, as one worthy of worship, and as one who would die, though Matthew does not explain them.

The star has been explained in several ways: a conjunction of the planets Jupiter and Saturn in 7 BC (a suggestion made by the astronomer Johannes Kepler), a comet or a nova recorded by Chinese astronomers around 5 BC, or a supernatural light, since the star moves ahead of the Magi and stops over a particular house. Ancient people widely believed that the births of great rulers were marked by signs in the heavens. The chapter also records that the family was living in a house by the time the Magi arrived, and Herod's order to kill boys two and under suggests that some months, perhaps a year or more, had passed since the birth.
literary: The chapter is a narrative in four scenes, each closed or shaped by a quotation from the prophets: Bethlehem (Micah 5:2, combined with 2 Samuel 5:2, verses 5 and 6), Egypt (Hosea 11:1, verse 15), Ramah (Jeremiah 31:15, verse 18), and Nazareth (verse 23). Three dreams guide Joseph, as in chapter 1, and a fourth warns the Magi, so that the action is directed from heaven while Herod plots on earth. The story is built on contrasts: two kings, a false worshiper (Herod says he wants to worship) and true ones (the Magi fall down and worship), scribes who know the Scriptures and do nothing, and foreigners who follow a star and find the Messiah. Readers familiar with Exodus notice echoes of Moses, who was also saved as a baby when a king killed Israelite boys, and who returned to his people after being told that those seeking his life were dead (compare Exodus 4:19 with verse 20).

outline.t: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem
Herod consults the scribes and sends the Magi to Bethlehem
The Magi worship the child and go home another way
Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
The return and the settling in Nazareth

doctrines.note: Jesus is born King of the Jews in David's town, as the prophets said. Matthew sets his true kingship against Herod's violent, fearful kingship.
God guides events through a star, dreams, and the timing of Herod's death, protecting the child without removing the danger. Providence here works through flight and exile, not only through miracle.
The first people in Matthew to worship Jesus are Gentiles from the east. The Gospel that ends with a command to disciple all nations begins with the nations coming to the king.

words.note: Magos, a sage or Magus. Elsewhere in the New Testament the word describes a sorcerer (Acts 13:6-8), and Judaism regarded astrology with suspicion. That makes the Magi's role here striking: people from outside Israel's covenant, using the means they had, are led by God to the Messiah.

Aster, star. Numbers 24:17 had spoken of a star coming out of Jacob and a scepter rising from Israel, a text Jews of the period read of a coming ruler. Matthew does not quote it, but many readers think it stands in the background of His star.

Proskyneo, to bow down, pay homage, or worship. It can describe honor paid to a king, but Matthew uses it repeatedly of people before Jesus (2:11; 14:33; 28:9, 17), and in 4:10 Jesus says worship belongs to God alone. The word begins the pattern here.

Nazoraios, Nazarene, a man from Nazareth. No Old Testament verse contains the phrase He will be called a Nazarene, and Matthew says prophets, plural. Suggested links include the Hebrew netser, branch, used of David's heir in Isaiah 11:1, and the obscurity of Nazareth, which fits prophecies that the Messiah would be despised.

christ: Matthew shows Jesus as the true king and the true Israel. The chief priests and scribes quote Micah: “But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.” Jesus is that shepherd-king from David's town. The quotation Out of Egypt I called My Son comes from Hosea 11:1, where it looks back to the exodus and speaks of Israel as God's son. Matthew is not claiming Hosea predicted this event; he is saying that Jesus relives and fulfills Israel's story as the Son in whom that sonship reaches its goal. Jeremiah's picture of Rachel weeping for her children is taken from a chapter about exile that moves immediately to hope and the promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:16-17, 31-34), and Matthew places the grief of Bethlehem's mothers inside that same hope. The Magi's worship anticipates the end of the Gospel, when all nations will be called to follow him.

hard.q: Why would God protect Jesus but allow the children of Bethlehem to be killed?
hard.a: Matthew does not explain it, and he does not make the massacre small. He quotes Jeremiah's image of Rachel weeping and refusing to be comforted, letting the grief stand. Several things can be said honestly. The evil is Herod's, not God's; Matthew consistently presents Herod as the one who plots and kills. The escape of Jesus is not a sign that God values some children and not others but part of a story in which the rescued child will himself die violently at the hands of rulers, sharing the suffering of the innocent rather than being exempt from it. And the Jeremiah passage Matthew cites continues with the promise that there is hope for the future and that the children will return, a hope Christians see fulfilled in the resurrection. This does not answer every question about why God permits such evil, a question Scripture itself raises in the Psalms, Job, and Lamentations, but it shows that Matthew does not pretend the question away.

questions: The scribes knew where the Messiah would be born but stayed put, while the Magi traveled far on less information. What keeps people who know a great deal about God from coming to him?
Herod saw the child as a threat to his power. In what ways can Jesus' kingship feel threatening to the things we control?
Jesus' family became refugees in Egypt. How might that shape the way Christians think about refugees and displaced people today?
